name: Wendy Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I look after the lines on the Porthaven peninsula and the two little islands off it. Some days that's a ferry crossing with the van at seven, a pole that's leaning after a winter of salt wind, and back on the last boat at six. Other days it's clearing gorse and branches off the lines with a pole saw. The salt eats everything out here, so there's always something to fix.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How do you find your way round the network?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The line book. It's a fat binder of paper maps with my pencil notes on every page, where the old joints are, which farmer's dog bites, which pole has a wasps' nest every August. The company gave us a tablet with a map on it, and I keep it in the glovebox, switched off. My book hasn't let me down in twenty-eight years.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Ray, my husband, fishes for crab and lobster from a small boat, so some months are good and some are nothing. Our daughter cuts hair in town and our son's in the army. We've got maybe three weeks of money put by, and the pay out here is lower than in the city depots. If this job went, there's nothing like it on the peninsula, it's just me and Lewis covering the whole patch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, and get on with it. I don't argue about this stuff online, I'm not on it. If someone asked at the café, I'd say a computer was never going to fix a pole on an island in a gale.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I keep going till sixty-six and then I'm done. That's the plan and it's not a fancy one. I've never been one for big changes and this would suit me down to the ground.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Keep the line book up to date, keep the van on the ferry, take the overtime in the winter storms. Maybe I'd finally put a little away each month, twenty or thirty, now that I'm not worrying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a flat sea in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about your job that worries you anyway, AI or not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The salt and my shoulders, mainly. My right shoulder clicks when I lift the saw above my head, and I don't tell anyone. If that goes, the job goes, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you talk to about it, if you were worried?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lewis, my crew mate, and Ray. Not the company. The company only phones when something's broken.

S0.say: I'd say there you go and get on with it, because I don't argue about this online. At the café I'd say a computer was never going to fix a pole on an island in a gale.
S0.think: Privately, it means I keep going to sixty-six and then stop, which is a plain plan that suits me. My bigger worry is my shoulder, not AI.
S0.do: Carries on as normal, keeps her paper line book up to date and takes winter storm overtime. Starts putting twenty or thirty a month aside.
S0.feel: Calm, like a flat sea in the morning.
S0.quote: My right shoulder clicks when I lift the saw above my head, and I don't tell anyone.
S0.fieldNote: Wendy's world is very local and practical, organised around a paper line book and the ferry timetable. She keeps the company tablet switched off in the glovebox. Her honest worry is her body, which she hides from her employer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, let's see what it actually does before we all lose our heads. Every few years there's some new system that's going to change everything, and half of them end up in a cupboard. I'd keep my head down and do my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, this is the one that'd get me. Not robots on the islands, but the computer side: a system that sends the jobs, a map I'd have to use, reports on a screen. If they decide the line book is out and the tablet is in, I'd be the one who can't keep up, and they'd notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start cutting back straight away, because if it goes bad I want a few more weeks in the bank. Ray and I would skip the trip to see our son at the base this year. I'd keep doing my job the way I do it and wait to see what they actually bring in, but I'd ask Lewis to show me the tablet on the quiet, so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. A knot in the chest that sits there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why on the quiet, rather than asking for training?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because if I ask for training, the supervisor writes it down that I can't use it. Lewis won't make a fuss. He's thirty-four and he thinks it's funny that I call it 'the gadget', but he's kind about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your patch if they merge depots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then it's run from the city, an hour and a ferry away. They talked about it in 2019 and dropped it. If it happens, they might keep Lewis and send me to the big depot, and I can't do that drive every day at my age.

S1.say: I'd say let's see what it actually does before we lose our heads, since half these new systems end up in a cupboard. I'd keep my head down and do my job.
S1.think: This is the one that would get me, through the computer side rather than robots: jobs sent by a system, a map on a screen, digital reports. If the line book is out and the tablet is in, I'd be the one who can't keep up.
S1.do: Cuts back right away and skips this year's trip to visit her son at his army base. Waits to see what the company brings in while asking her crew mate to teach her the tablet quietly.
S1.feel: Anxious, with a knot in her chest that won't shift.
S1.quote: If they decide the line book is out and the tablet is in, I'd be the one who can't keep up, and they'd notice.
S1.fieldNote: Even mild change hits Wendy hard because her skills are tied to paper and memory, and she has no savings and no other local job. She'd learn the tablet secretly rather than admit she needs training. The fear of a depot merger runs underneath everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably nothing at first, I'd just go quiet. If someone pushed me at the café I'd say somebody should have seen this coming, the government or the companies, I don't care which.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished. Sixty, a shoulder that clicks, three weeks of money, a husband with a boat that earns nothing in February. There's no other line job here and I'm not moving off the peninsula, so I don't know what that leaves.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything that isn't food, heating or the boat's fuel. I'd help Ray sell his catch straight to people on the quay instead of through the dealer, to get a bit more for it. And I'd have to ask our daughter if she could help with the bills, which I've never done. I'd take early retirement if they offered it, even a bad one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ferry's left and I'm still on the slipway with the van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it make a difference that robots would have to manage island work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, maybe. But I wouldn't count on it. Someone in an office would decide the islands were too expensive to keep a person on, and send a robot over twice a year instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Ray, that first evening?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't tell him straight away. I'd make tea and talk about the weather and his pots. Then the next morning, on the slipway, I'd tell him, because that's where we talk about anything serious.

S2.say: At first I'd probably go quiet and say nothing. If pushed at the café, I'd say somebody should have seen it coming, the government or the companies.
S2.think: I'd be finished: sixty, a bad shoulder, three weeks of money and a husband whose boat earns nothing in February. There's no other line job here and I won't leave the peninsula.
S2.do: Cuts everything except food, heating and the boat's fuel, and helps her husband sell his catch directly on the quay. Asks her daughter for help with bills and takes early retirement if it's offered, even on poor terms.
S2.feel: Stranded and helpless, as if the ferry had left without her.
S2.quote: Like the ferry's left and I'm still on the slipway with the van.
S2.fieldNote: Wendy has no slack anywhere: no savings, no second trade, no other local employer and no willingness to move. She doesn't pick a villain, which fits her middle-of-the-road outlook. Telling her husband on the slipway rather than at home is a small, telling ritual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning, so the company had better tell us what the plan is. I'm not one for marches, but I'd want a straight answer. I'd ask for one at the next depot meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-three. That's close to sixty-six but not close enough. Three years without pay would empty us out twice over. Still, it's better than two, I can see that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start putting fifty a month away from the first month, which would hurt. I'd ask Lewis to teach me the tablet properly, not just on the quiet. And I'd ask about any part-time or call-out role near the end, so I can stretch to the pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened. But it's frightened with a plan, not frightened with nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the extra time let you do that two years didn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the gadget, mostly. If I've got five years I can get used to it, slowly, the way I learned the islands. In two years I'd just be lost.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't move off the peninsula. Would five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. Ray's boat is here, my mother's buried here. If I'm going to struggle, I'd rather struggle here than in a flat in the city.

S3.say: I'd say five years is a decent warning, so the company should tell us the plan. I'm not one for marches, but I'd ask for a straight answer at the next depot meeting.
S3.think: I'd be sixty-three, close to the pension but not close enough, and three years without pay would empty us twice over. It's still better than two years.
S3.do: Starts saving fifty a month from the first month and asks her crew mate to teach her the tablet properly. Asks about a part-time or call-out role near the end to stretch to the pension.
S3.quote: It's frightened with a plan, not frightened with nothing.
S3.fieldNote: Five years gives Wendy just enough time to learn the tablet slowly, the way she learned the islands. She still won't move, because her husband's boat and her mother's grave keep her there. Her ask is simple: a straight answer from the company.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for them to sort it out, so they'd better. I'd still not be posting about it. I'd just get on with my job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be sixty-eight, retired two years. If I can keep the shoulder going to sixty-six, it's someone else's problem by then. That sounds hard, but it's honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep working to sixty-six. Put a bit away each month. Teach whoever comes after me the islands, maybe give them the line book, if they'd even want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a bit. It's the shoulder more than anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you hand over the line book?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to. Twenty-eight years of notes in pencil. Probably they'd scan it into the computer and the robot would read it, which is a funny thought.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you most in those ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I don't make it to sixty-six with my body in one piece. If I break before the job does, all this planning is no good.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for them to sort it out, so they'd better. I still wouldn't post about it and would just get on with my job.
S4.think: I'd be sixty-eight and retired for two years, so if my shoulder lasts to sixty-six it's someone else's problem. That sounds hard, but it's honest.
S4.do: Keeps working to sixty-six and puts a bit aside each month. Plans to teach her successor the islands and hand over her paper line book.
S4.feel: Slightly uneasy, mainly about her shoulder.
S4.quote: Probably they'd scan it into the computer and the robot would read it, which is a funny thought.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, the technology stops being Wendy's main threat and her body takes over. She is blunt that the change would become someone else's problem. Handing over the line book matters to her more than she lets on.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. What would help is someone keeping the islands staffed by a person till I'm sixty-six, or paying me to sixty-six if they won't. And training that doesn't get written down as a black mark.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could ask about the places at the end of the line. Everyone talks about the cities. Out here, if the one person goes, the lights stay off a lot longer.

headlineQuote: Out here, if the one person goes, the lights stay off a lot longer.
portrait: Wendy Usman is a fifty-eight-year-old lineworker who covers a salty coastal peninsula and two small islands by ferry, using a paper line book of pencil notes instead of the company tablet. Her husband fishes for crab and lobster, their savings would last about three weeks, and there's no other line job nearby. She is practical and unpolitical, blames no one in particular and hides a clicking shoulder from her employer. She is calm when AI fizzles, already anxious with steady change because of the computer side, and panicked by AGI in two years. With more warning time she plans to learn the tablet slowly and hold on to sixty-six.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because at sixty she'd have no money, no other local line work and no intention of leaving the peninsula.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping a person on the islands until she is sixty-six or paying her until then, and training that isn't recorded as a black mark.
